title: A First-Timer's Esports & Gaming Culture Tour of Seoul: 2 Nights, 3 Days Itinerary
html:
South Korea is often called the "esports capital of the world," and it's not just a slogan — this is the country that invented the PC bang (PC방, literally "computer room"), turned StarCraft into a national pastime in the 1990s, and still produces some of the best professional League of Legends and Valorant players on the planet. You don't need to be a hardcore gamer to enjoy this side of Korea; you just need curiosity and a T-money transit card. This 2-night, 3-day route is built for complete beginners: no Korean required, no gaming gear to bring, and everything reachable by subway.

A quick heads-up before you start: gaming venues in Korea open, rebrand, and close faster than most tourist attractions — one famous esports arena even changed its own name partway through 2026. Prices and hours below are a solid starting point, but it's worth a quick search the night before to confirm nothing has changed.

Day 1 Morning & Afternoon: Hongdae — Your First PC Bang, Plus a Pro Team's Fan Lounge

Start in Hongdae, the university neighborhood around Hongik University that's also one of Seoul's biggest clusters of gaming spots. Walk into any PC bang — look for a sign with "PC" on it — and you'll find rows of high-spec gaming PCs, usually open 24 hours. You don't need to speak Korean or download an app: most PC bangs now have a self-service kiosk at the entrance with an English option. Pick "non-member" (비회원), pay with cash or a card, and the kiosk prints a seat number. Standard PC bangs charge around ₩1,000–2,000 per hour; as a non-member tourist, expect closer to ₩2,000–3,000 per hour, sometimes sold in 2-hour blocks. Locals almost always sign up for a cheap membership to get the lower rate — as a short-term visitor, the non-member kiosk option is the easier path. While you're at your seat, try ordering a snack from the in-house menu; cheap ramyeon (instant noodles) and sweet iced coffee delivered straight to your keyboard is a classic part of the experience.

A few minutes' walk away, near Hongdae Station, is T1 Base Camp, a gaming lounge run by T1 — the esports team behind the world-famous League of Legends player Faker. It's part PC bang, part fan museum: expect premium gaming PCs, a merchandise shop, a lounge area, and big screens that show T1's matches live when the team is playing. Non-member pricing is reportedly higher than a regular PC bang (budget roughly ₩3,000 or more per hour — confirm on-site, as this isn't officially published), but you're paying for the atmosphere and the photo ops as much as the PC itself. T1 has since opened a second Base Camp in Gangnam and one in Busan too, so if Hongdae doesn't fit your route, you can catch one elsewhere.


A street in Hongdae, home to some of Seoul's busiest PC bangs and gaming lounges. Photo: U0894629, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Day 1 Evening: VR Arcades and Board Game Cafes

Once you've had enough of sitting at a PC, Hongdae also has plenty of other ways to play. VR arcades are small, walk-in venues where staff strap you into a headset for horror, shooting, or sports games — no experience needed, and most sessions run about 30–70 minutes for roughly ₩10,000–20,000. If you'd rather sit down with friends, Hongdae is also full of board game cafes (보드게임 카페) stocked with hundreds of games, most with English rules or simple enough to pick up without reading anything. Pricing is usually a flat unlimited-play fee for the whole visit — often ₩6,000–8,000 on weekdays, a bit more on weekends — and staff will teach you a game if you ask. Most of these spots are same-day walk-in only, so there's nothing to book in advance.


The park-lined streets near Hongdae Station, where many of the area's VR arcades and board game cafes cluster. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — source.

Day 2 Morning: Dongdaemun — Gen.G's GGX Gaming Hub

Take the subway to Dongdaemun History & Culture Park Station (lines 2, 4, and 5) — the same stop you'd use for the famous DDP building — and look for GGX, short for "Gen.G Gaming Experience." Gen.G is another major Korean esports organization, and GGX is their huge public gaming hall: about 1,570 square meters with 252 gaming stations, plus a food and drink lounge, a merchandise store, and a photo zone with the team mascot. It opened in 2025 specifically to welcome both local fans and foreign tourists, so don't feel shy walking in without a Korean friend to translate. Interestingly, GGX and Hongdae's T1 Base Camp are both operated by the same company, Superplay, which explains why the two venues feel like siblings.


Dongdaemun Design Plaza, right next to the same subway station you'll use to reach GGX. Photo: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — source.

Day 2 Afternoon: Yongsan Electronics Market — Korea's Original Tech Town

From Dongdaemun, head to Yongsan Station and the sprawling Yongsan Electronics Market next door — a maze of multi-story buildings crammed with shops selling computer parts, consoles, retro games, and secondhand electronics. It's less polished than a department store, so bargaining is normal and not every shop takes card, but it's a fascinating, low-cost browse even if you're not buying anything. The district has been Korea's electronics hub since the 1980s, and in 2026 the city approved a major redevelopment plan to turn the area into an AI and tech content district, so parts of it may look different on your next visit — all the more reason to see the old-school version while it's still here. Nearby, the I'Park Mall has also been adding pop-up stores tied to gaming and other subcultures, worth a peek if you have extra time.


Yongsan Station, right next to the Yongsan Electronics Market. Photo: Mobius6, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Day 3: Watch a Pro Match at CHZZK LoL Park, Then Wrap Up at COEX

For your last day, head to Jonggak Station in central Seoul to find CHZZK LoL Park (renamed from "LoL Park" in late 2025), the dedicated arena where Korea's professional League of Legends league, the LCK, plays its matches. It sits on the 3rd floor of the Gran Seoul building. The arena is small — capacity is only around 400–450 seats — so tickets for live matches (sold through Interpark or NOL) can sell out fast; check the LCK schedule before you plan your trip, since matches aren't held every day. Even without a match ticket, the venue's exhibition area is sometimes open to walk through, but hours vary, so confirm on NAVER Map first.

If there's no match or the exhibition is closed, spend the rest of the day at COEX in Gangnam instead (or combine both if you have time — they're about 20–30 minutes apart by subway). Besides being home to the famous Starfield Library, COEX's Gangnam neighborhood is also where T1 opened its newest Base Camp location, so it's a fitting place to end a gaming-themed trip with one more round at a PC — or just a well-earned coffee.


Photo: COEX complex, Gangnam, Seoul, via Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr).

Which Gaming Spot Should You Pick?

Here's a quick comparison if you're short on time and need to choose just one or two:

Venue typeTypical priceTypical visit lengthBest for
Regular PC bang₩1,000–2,000/hr (member); ₩2,000–3,000/hr (non-member)1–3 hoursAn authentic, budget-friendly taste of everyday Korean gaming culture
Pro-team lounge (T1 Base Camp, GGX)From roughly ₩3,000/hr, plus merch2–4 hoursFans of a specific team, premium PCs, photo spots
VR arcade~₩10,000–20,000 per session30–70 minutesGroups, zero gaming skill required
Board game cafe~₩6,000–8,000 flat (unlimited play)2–3 hoursLow-key hangouts, no Korean needed
CHZZK LoL Park (live match)Ticket price varies; sells out fast2–3 hoursEsports fans who want to see pros play in person

💬 Found a gaming spot in Korea we should know about, or have a question before your trip? Drop it in the comments — happy to help!
meta_description: A beginner-friendly 2-night, 3-day Seoul itinerary: PC bangs, pro esports lounges, VR arcades, board game cafes, and a live LCK match.
